knowledgeBase.name: AnyBank FAQs
knowledgeBase.description: Answers general questions about everyday banking at AnyBank: fees, overdraft, disputes, transfer and wire timing, lost or stolen cards, payment limits, and bill pay. Holds no customer records.

question.text: What fees does my account charge, and how do I avoid them?

responses.body: Checking accounts carry a twelve dollar monthly service fee, and it is waived in any month where you either keep a fifteen hundred dollar minimum daily balance, receive a qualifying direct deposit of five hundred dollars or more, or hold Gold, Platinum or higher status. Savings accounts have no monthly fee. The fees people actually run into are the ones tied to a single event rather than to the month: thirty-four dollars for an overdraft, twelve dollars for a returned item, three dollars at an out-of-network cash machine plus whatever the machine's owner charges, and twenty-five dollars for an outgoing domestic wire. There is no fee for a transfer between your own accounts, for standard bill pay, for locking or unlocking a card, or for filing a dispute. Statements are free electronically; a paper statement is two dollars a month.

question.text: How does overdraft work, and what is overdraft protection?

responses.body: An overdraft happens when a payment or a card charge is more than your available balance and we pay it anyway. When that happens the fee is thirty-four dollars, and no more than three of them can be charged in one day. Two things reduce that. First, we do not charge an overdraft fee on any item of five dollars or less, and we do not charge one if your account ends the day no more than fifty dollars negative. Second, overdraft protection links your checking account to another account you hold, usually savings, and pulls the shortfall across automatically instead of overdrawing; that transfer is free. Overdraft protection is something you switch on per account and it can be added or removed at any time. Worth knowing the difference between the two balances you will hear: the posted balance is what has settled, and the available balance is what you can actually spend right now, which is lower while a charge is still pending. Overdraft is judged against the available balance.

question.text: How long does a dispute take, and do I get the money back while you investigate?

responses.body: Once a dispute is filed we acknowledge it within one business day and then have ten business days to investigate. If the investigation is going to take longer than that, we issue a provisional credit for the disputed amount within those ten business days so you are not out of pocket while we work, and we then have up to forty-five days in total to finish, or ninety days if the charge was made outside the country or at a point of sale rather than online. You keep the provisional credit unless the investigation finds the charge was legitimate, and if that happens we tell you in writing before it is reversed, with at least five days' notice. Report an unauthorised charge as soon as you notice it: your liability is capped at fifty dollars if you tell us within two business days of the statement, and reporting promptly is what keeps it there. Filing a dispute does not stop the card being used again, so if the charge was fraud rather than a mistake, lock the card as well.

question.text: When does a transfer actually move, and what are the wire cut-off times?

responses.body: A transfer between two accounts you hold with us is immediate and free, at any hour, on any day. Everything that leaves the bank has a cut-off. A standard transfer to an account you hold elsewhere takes one to three business days and has to be submitted by eight in the evening Eastern time to start that day. A domestic wire has to be in by five in the evening Eastern time on a business day and lands the same day; an international wire has to be in by three in the afternoon Eastern time and takes one to two business days. Anything submitted after the cut-off, at a weekend or on a public holiday starts on the next business day. Wires cannot be recalled once they have been sent, which is the reason we read the details back before submitting one; a standard transfer that has not left yet can still be cancelled.

question.text: My card is missing: should I lock it or replace it?

responses.body: Lock it first. Locking is instant, free and completely reversible: it stops new purchases, cash withdrawals and any attempt to add the card to a digital wallet, while letting your existing direct debits and recurring subscriptions keep running so nothing you rely on fails. If the card turns up in a coat pocket you unlock it and carry on with the same card number. Replacing is different. A replacement cancels the card number for good, so it is the right choice when the card was stolen, when it is damaged, or when you are confident it is gone. A replacement card arrives in five to seven business days, or one to two if you ask for it to be expedited, and it is free either way. Because the old number dies, anything set up to charge that card, such as a subscription, a season ticket, or a wallet on your phone, has to be pointed at the new one, and that is worth knowing before you choose. If money has already gone out of the account, locking or replacing the card does not by itself get it back; that is a dispute, and it is a separate step.

question.text: Is there a limit on how much I can transfer or pay in one go?

responses.body: Between your own accounts here there is no limit beyond the available balance in the account the money is leaving. Everything else has one. A standard transfer to an account elsewhere is capped at five thousand dollars a day and fifteen thousand dollars a month. Bill pay is capped at ten thousand dollars for a single payment. A domestic wire is capped at fifty thousand dollars a day online, and above that it has to be done with a banker. Card spending has its own separate limits: two thousand dollars a day on debit purchases and five hundred dollars a day in cash withdrawals, and those reset at midnight local time. Platinum status raises the transfer and wire limits. A limit can be lifted temporarily for something specific like a house deposit or a car, but that has to be arranged with a banker rather than switched on in the moment.

question.text: When does a bill payment actually reach the payee, and can I cancel one?

responses.body: A payment submitted before eight in the evening Eastern time on a business day is sent that day. How quickly it lands depends on the payee: most large ones are paid electronically and post in one to two business days, and a smaller payee we have to pay by cheque takes four to five. That is why the guidance is to schedule a payment at least three business days before its due date rather than on the day. The money leaves your account on the date the payment is scheduled for, not on the day the payee posts it. A scheduled payment can be cancelled any time before its send date, at no charge, and a repeating payment can be cancelled or changed up to the day before the next one goes. Once a payment has been sent it cannot be cancelled; if it went to the wrong payee or for the wrong amount at that point, it becomes a claim rather than a cancellation, and that needs a person.

question.text: How do I reach a person, and when are you open?

responses.body: General support is on the phone from seven in the morning to ten in the evening Eastern time, seven days a week. Two lines never close: the fraud and lost-card line, which is staffed twenty-four hours a day every day of the year, and the automated service in the app and on the phone, which can check balances, move money between your own accounts and lock a card at any hour. Branches are open nine to five on weekdays and nine to one on Saturdays, closed Sundays and public holidays, and an appointment is worth making for anything to do with a loan, a mortgage or an account opening. Some things need a person by design rather than by opening hours, including anything about a loan or a mortgage, opening or closing an account, raising a limit, a payment sent to the wrong payee, a wire that has already gone, and any question about what you should do with your money rather than what your account currently says.
